candidato.titulo: In a first, ultrasound maps blood flow through an entire human kidney in 3D
candidato.resumo: For the first time, a research team at the Inserm Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS) in Paris has succeeded in visualizing the entire vascular network and blood flow in a human kidney. This breakthrough opens up promising clinical prospects: improving our understanding and diagnosis of kidney diseases linked to vascular defects. To achieve this, the researchers used a new ultrasound technique developed in their laboratory and previously tested in animals, which could eventually be extended to other organs. The results are published in The Lancet Medical Imaging & Theranostics.

texto_fonte:
In a first, ultrasound maps blood flow through an entire human kidney in 3D
For the first time, a research team at the Inserm Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS) in Paris has succeeded in visualizing the entire vascular network and blood flow in a human kidney. This breakthrough opens up promising clinical prospects: improving our understanding and diagnosis of kidney diseases linked to vascular defects. To achieve this, the researchers used a new ultrasound technique developed in their laboratory and previously tested in animals, which could eventually be extended to other organs. The results are published in The Lancet Medical Imaging & Theranostics.
The proper functioning of an organ depends closely on its vascular network. When arteries or veins are abnormal, the cells' needs for oxygen and nutrients are not met as effectively, and cellular waste is not eliminated as efficiently. The organs then suffer.
The kidney is particularly affected: changes in its microvasculature play a major role in many kidney diseases. This is particularly true of hypertensive nephrosclerosis and diabetic nephropathy, which are characterized by progressive damage to the small arteries and arterioles of the kidney, contributing to the loss of its filtration function.
"Currently, there is no specific biomarker that can directly detect these vascular abnormalities and monitor their progression. And the imaging techniques currently used cannot visualize the affected arterioles, whether it be conventional ultrasound—which lacks sufficient resolution—or MRI and CT scans," explains Clément Papadacci, an Inserm research fellow and team leader at the Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS).
Consequently, in the absence of early diagnosis and intervention, the disease is a major contributor to the development of kidney failure, requiring patients to undergo dialysis.
Directly observing the small blood vessels involved in kidney diseases is therefore a major challenge for clinicians. It is for this purpose, among others, that the team has developed a new ultrasound technique in recent years. By combining several innovations, they have developed an ultrasound probe that makes it possible to visualize the entire vascular system of an organ in three dimensions—down to the smallest capillaries—and to track blood flow in real time.
This is a remarkable achievement, given that some vessels are 50 micrometers in diameter—the size of a fine hair—and that conventional ultrasound can only visualize vessels 1 to 2 millimeters in diameter, or the size of the head of a pin.
The team has already demonstrated the effectiveness of this tool in animals for visualizing the vascular system of kidneys—and even entire hearts and livers. Now, they have demonstrated its feasibility in humans.
For the first time, the team is providing images of entire kidneys along with quantitative data on the organ's complete vascular architecture—from the largest arteries down to the microvessels—and the blood flow within each vessel. The system also allows the organ to be segmented to focus on areas of interest, or to separate venous and arterial blood flow for separate study.
"Beyond its technological capabilities, this new generation of ultrasound technology could lead to significant advances in research and medicine. In the case of hypertensive nephrosclerosis in particular, our device could help us not only better understand the condition but also, likely, identify early biomarkers to improve diagnosis," explains Hannah Plath, a doctoral student at the Institute of Physics for Medicine (Inserm/ESPCI Paris-PSL/CNRS) and the study's first author.
This new generation of ultrasound could well contribute to our understanding of other types of diseases, since, in principle, all organs can be observed in their entirety and with their full vascular complexity.
In a clinical trial, the team will monitor blood flow in the kidneys, as well as in the brain and heart, of patients with atherosclerosis who are candidates for complex surgery.
"This surgical procedure alters blood flow and can compromise these organs. The clinical study aims to predict potential risks for patients," explains Papadacci, who led the research.
How does ultra-high-definition ultrasound imaging of an entire organ work?
To visualize an entire organ with high precision, researchers have developed an ultrasound probe that is much larger than a conventional probe and incorporates numerous components. Acoustic lenses, in particular, are responsible for focusing sound waves with great precision. This probe makes it possible to explore a large volume in three dimensions with high resolution thanks to very high-speed image acquisition.
Finally, microbubbles injected into the bloodstream and carried along by blood flow reveal even the smallest vessels. The combination of these innovations thus makes it possible to achieve two capabilities that were previously difficult to combine: viewing an entire organ and distinguishing its microvasculature.
More information
Hannah Plath et al., Whole-organ mapping of renal microcirculatory haemodynamics in vivo using three-dimensional ultrasound localisation microscopy: a first-in-human feasibility study, The Lancet Medical Imaging & Theranostics (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.lanmit.2026.100039

candidato.titulo: Why fertile male killifish outlive their peers
candidato.resumo: Why do some individuals of the same species live significantly longer than others? In evolutionary biology and aging research, this question is often linked to a trade-off between reproduction and survival. The underlying idea is that energy and resources invested in reproduction may lead to compromises in repair and maintenance, thereby hindering a long life. Thus, the assumption is that particularly successful reproduction at a young age comes at the cost of a shorter lifespan.

texto_fonte:
Why fertile male killifish outlive their peers
Why do some individuals of the same species live significantly longer than others? In evolutionary biology and aging research, this question is often linked to a trade-off between reproduction and survival. The underlying idea is that energy and resources invested in reproduction may lead to compromises in repair and maintenance, thereby hindering a long life. Thus, the assumption is that particularly successful reproduction at a young age comes at the cost of a shorter lifespan.
Researchers at the Leibniz Institute on Aging–Fritz Lipmann Institute (FLI) in Jena, Dr. Silvia Cattelan and professor Dario Riccardo Valenzano, have now investigated this hypothesis in more detail and examined the question using the turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri), a naturally short-lived fish. This fish is increasingly adopted as a model organism for aging research because it allows researchers to study the in vivo biology of aging within a period of just a few months.
The study results have now been published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B: Biological Sciences, as a part of a special issue entitled "Developmental circuits in ageing."
In order to assess reproductive performance across different life stages, the researchers studied male turquoise killifish using a systematic approach. To this end, ejaculates were collected repeatedly throughout the animals' lifespans, and actual reproductive performance was determined after in vitro fertilization. In a subsequent step, the reproductive outcomes were correlated with individual lifespan. In addition, the researchers developed a comprehensive statistical model that recapitulates and helps interpret the relationship between reproduction and survival. The age-related decline in reproductive performance was also taken into account.
"It's been great fun to work on this project with Silvia—we had extensive discussions about the results that at first were puzzling and were challenging a long-standing dogma. The most important results could only be obtained through the combination of Silvia's expertise in male fish reproductive aging and my modeling approach using a Bayesian causal inference framework," explains Valenzano, group leader and scientific director at the FLI. The model was able to largely reproduce the observed results when it accounted for a common intrinsic quality as a factor influencing reproduction and lifespan.
Early reproductive success predicts a longer life
The study contradicts the assumption that reproductive success early in life predicts a short lifespan. In the male fish studied, higher reproductive success at an early age was an honest predictor of higher father quality. In fact, fathers with higher reproductive success in early life lived longer on average.
"What's striking about our finding is that since father reproductive fitness predicts lifespan, measuring reproductive success in young fathers could be used as a bona fide proxy for Darwinian fitness," explains Valenzano.
Individual biological quality as a key factor
The researchers therefore examined an alternative explanation: Individuals may differ in their intrinsic biological quality. If this quality is sufficiently high, they can reproduce more successfully. Conversely, these same individuals apparently also have better prospects for longer survival. Reproductive success and lifespan are thus two characteristics that are partly influenced by shared biological factors. In this context, reproductive performance could be understood as an indicator of general individual quality.
Whether the results obtained from male turquoise killifish can be directly extrapolated to females, other species or even humans must be clarified in further studies.
"What I found exciting is that just by using the ejaculate of these males, we can capture their overall quality as individuals. We still don't know what this quality is made of, and finding out, in males as well as in females, is one of the next questions we want to address," says Cattelan, first author of the study.
Search for common biological causes
The results suggest that differences in lifespan should not be understood exclusively as the result of a trade-off between reproduction and self-preservation. Rather, some of the differences could be due to the fact that certain individuals have more favorable biological conditions from the outset—or throughout their lives. Reproductive success is then not necessarily the cause of a longer lifespan, but rather a measurable indicator of an individual's differing initial biological quality.
This would also have broader implications for aging research: If we wish to understand why some individuals live longer and healthier lives than others, we may need to focus more on identifying common biological causes underlying health, reproductive capacity and survival.
Publication details
Silvia Cattelan et al., Early-life reproductive success predicts lifespan: intrinsic quality, not reproductive trade-offs, explains heterogeneity in a short-lived vertebrate, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences (2026). DOI: 10.1098/rstb.2025.0324

candidato.titulo: GXO doubling down on robotics in 2027
candidato.resumo: GXO didn't disclose which providers it would increase deployments with, but let's take a look at the existing technologies in its portfolio. The post GXO doubling down on robotics in 2027 appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
GXO Logistics plans to accelerate deployments of adaptive technologies across the U.S. in 2027. The phased rollout will start at GXO’s priority sites and continue over the next 12 months.
The deployment will include:
- Pallet AMRs to automate repetitive material transport and improve warehouse and production flow.
- Robotic arms deployable across multiple applications including inbound unloading and packing solutions.
- AI-enabled vision technologies to enable hands-free data capture, improving productivity and inventory checks.
- Flexible and scalable automated sortation systems.
“Today’s supply chains require solutions that are efficient and adaptable,” said Michael Jacobs, CEO of the Americas & Asia Pacific at GXO. “This deployment underscores our commitment to helping customers modernize their operations with technologies that can deliver immediate value while positioning them for long-term growth. By leveraging advanced automation and vision-enabled solutions across multiple industries, we are enabling safer, smarter and more responsive operations across our footprint.”
GXO said it expects the deployments to help sites increase efficiency, optimize labor resources, and enhance service levels. The company didn’t disclose which providers it would be sourcing these robots from, but let’s take a look at the existing technologies in its portfolio.
GXO continues investing in humanoids
Earlier this month, GXO shared it is expanding its partnership with Apptronik. The partners are working toward a global rollout of up to 1,000 Apollo humanoids over the next four years. Jeff Cardenas, co-founder and CEO of Apptronik, said in an interview with investment firm RoboStrategy that, when the company started working with GXO in 2024, it tested a range of tasks to see what Apollo would be best at. Eventually, the companies landed on logistics tasks, like kitting.
“We measured the performance of the model against a benchmark, which is basically a human benchmark, and we showed that the model could perform 96% efficient for those tasks,” Cardenas said.
Under the agreement, Apptronik said that it and GXO will expand joint trials of Apollo in live operations across a range of warehouse workflows. These include goods-to-person (G2P) and person-to-goods picking, case and tote movement, packing, and sortation.
“Where humanoids are at today is we’re proving out the KPIs,” Cardenas said. “Can we actually do these tasks with an ROI that makes sense? Then, once you do that, you really get into site acceptance testing, where you can start to go from a handful of robots to the 1,000 units that we’re excited to deploy.”
This fall, GXO also expanded its deployments with Agility Robotics, another humanoid developer. GXO said it plans to deploy Agility’s Digit humanoids in its North Carolina and Tennessee sites. GXO first deployed Digit in late 2023 at a facility in Flowery Branch, Ga. Since then, Digit has moved more than 100,000 totes at the Flowery Branch facility, demonstrating its ability to perform repetitive material handling tasks in an active logistics environment.
GXO is also testing Reflex from Reflex Robotics, but hasn’t given an update on if it plans to expand those tests.
In the company’s second-quarter earnings call in August, GXO CEO Patrick Kelleher acknowledged humanoids had not yet produced a return on investment (ROI).
What other technology providers does GXO work with?
Outside of humanoids, GXO has deployed a range of other kinds of automation in its facilities. For example, the company has deployed Exotec Skypod system at its facility supporting global fashion brand Guess. Skypod is an automated storage and retrieval system (ASRS) that unified picking and packing.
Earlier this year, GXO deployed the Autoload system in Europe for Grupa Żywiec in Elbląg, one of the leading beer producers. GXO said the technology increases throughput, enhances workplace safety and elevates operational standards. The system automated trailer loading and unloading, replacing traditional forklift operations.
In 2025, the company deployed Dexory’s automatic inventory robot at its site in Oosterhout, Netherlands. It also had plans to expand deployments to the U.S. and the rest of Europe. DexoryView automates manual cycle counts and stock checks, which it said can help its customers save over 70% of labor time.

candidato.titulo: Netflix Builds Quasar to Measure the Blast Radius of Library API Changes
candidato.resumo: Netflix developed Quasar, an internal tool that combines semantic code indexing and API comparisons to identify downstream consumers affected by library changes. Using SCIP, Amazon S3, and Athena, it traces API references across repositories, helping maintainers assess migration impact and make informed release decisions. Netflix is also exploring agent-assisted consumer migrations. By Leela Kumili

texto_fonte:
Netflix has developed Quasar, an internal tool that identifies which repositories use specific library API symbols, helping engineering teams assess the downstream impact of proposed changes before releasing them. The tool combines semantic code indexing with API comparisons to identify affected consumers, dependency versions, and relevant call sites across repositories.
The challenge extends beyond identifying whether an API change is incompatible. Compatibility tools can flag a removed method or changed signature, but they do not necessarily identify which applications call it. Dependency graphs show declared relationships rather than actual usage, while text searches can miss references involving inheritance, overloads, and generated code. Building every downstream consumer to validate a change can also be expensive.
Quasar architecture diagram showing the indexing and query workflow (Source: Netflix Blog Post)
Quasar indexes symbol definitions and references using the SCIP Code Intelligence Protocol, an open format for representing code relationships. Language-specific indexers submit data during CI builds, which Quasar stores in Amazon S3 as Parquet files and queries through Amazon Athena.
During pull request analysis, Quasar compares API definitions between commits and identifies added, removed, or modified symbols. It then queries indexed references to locate affected repositories, dependency versions, and source locations. A Netflix example shows a deprecated method removal affecting 137 repositories across three library versions.
Example Quasar impact report showing affected repositories and dependency versions (Source: Netflix Blog Post)
However, an absence of indexed references does not prove that an API is unused. Reflection, dynamic loading, stale indexes, and incomplete coverage can prevent Quasar from observing every consumer.
Antonio J. del Águila, founder of Knaisoma, highlighted another limitation in a LinkedIn discussion about the approach:
Observed usage has a blind spot for reflection and for code on rare paths, like a quarterly batch job, since those calls may never show up in the window that was sampled.
Roberto Pérez Alcolea, a member of Netflix's Java Platform Team and author of the original article, acknowledged the limitation and described ongoing work to complement static evidence:
Reflection and incomplete indexing remain blind spots, and we’re also investing in runtime analysis to complement the static evidence. Together, those signals help inform removal decisions, without guaranteeing that an API is safe to delete.
Quasar complements Revapi for API compatibility analysis and Kythe for code navigation by connecting API changes with actual usage across repositories. SCIP supports usage queries across Java, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust, while compatibility analysis covers JVM APIs and Protobuf changes traced through generated Java code. Netflix exposes findings through REST, GraphQL, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for developers and coding agents.
Netflix plans to move impact analysis earlier into coding workflows, allowing agents to identify public API changes and retrieve consumer information before pull requests are opened. The goal is to help prepare migration changes while keeping API and release decisions with library producers.

candidato.titulo: Beijing’s AI ambitions are under threat as models may fall behind by up to nine months versus competitors — Chinese AI labs are under heavy fire from export controls, maturing chip stacks and a distillation crackdown
candidato.resumo: This week, several reports have detailed how closing GPU rental loopholes across Asia may have had an impact on the development of Chinese AI models.

texto_fonte:
This week, several reports have detailed how closing GPU rental loopholes across Asia may have had an impact on the development of Chinese AI models. In September, Mozilla estimated that open-weight AI models were three to six months behind the frontier. Since then, developments in the AI industry and export control rules could mean that Chinese AI models, many of which are typically open-weight, might fall even further behind Western counterparts, by up to nine months.
Zhipu AI, the developer of the GLM series of models, has allegedly pushed its release calendar back as a result of reduced access to advanced AI accelerators, Reuters said. It's an open secret that data centers located in Asia have been renting compute capacity to Chinese entities for some time. In light of the recent Nvidia scandal involving Jensen Huang and Megaspeed, the U.S. Department of Commerce has since tightened its rules over how data centers lend their compute capacity to Chinese entities. This has created an environment where there is, in fact, an excess of compute capacity available in the region, Bloomberg reported.
These curbs have a knock-on effect on how companies train their AI models, with Nvidia's AI accelerators being the most coveted; not having access to them stifles the development of AI in the region. However, this isn't entirely true across the industry. DeepSeek is attempting to wean itself off foreign silicon and instead adopting Huawei's Ascend AI chips, and porting its libraries away from CUDA and onto the open-source CANN. However, this hasn't stopped Chinese AI labs from facing another issue: tightened security against the distillation of AI models.
Distillation is a practice wherein the way a model thinks can be extracted and then learned from. It is largely believed to be the method in which Chinese AI labs have made great leaps in intelligence over the past several years, though several of China's leading labs refute that claim. The Western frontier has become more obtuse: Anthropic in October detailed how it's leveled up its own defences against distillation attacks, and the obfuscation of an AI model's chain of thought adds another hurdle. According to The Information, this is an issue that DeepSeek is now reportedly reckoning with. If distillation curbs the development of Chinese AI models even further, the gap between Eastern and Western frontier intelligence grows from three to six months to an estimated nine months.
The current standings
If you look at Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, which ranks AI models across a wide range of benchmarks and scores them in numerical order, Anthropic currently has the leading public AI model: Claude Fable 5.2, at a total of 65 points. Meanwhile, the leading Chinese AI model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, sits at 47. Between the two contenders are practically every Western frontier lab: OpenAI, Google, and Meta are all outgunning Chinese competitors, which were, just a few short months ago, competing at the frontier across many tasks.
It's important to mention that Artificial Analysis also changed its methodology over recent weeks, with China's AI models falling slightly further behind in added benchmarks, such as the Omniscience score, which tracks how often an AI is likely to hallucinate. This is paired with a jump in capability among the Western labs: Right now, it's on the Chinese AI labs' shoulders to respond in kind, and if current releases are anything to go by, they are falling short of expectations, especially in domains such as cybersecurity. An Epoch AI report characterized the difference in capabilities between GLM 5.3 and Claude Opus 5.5 as a six-to-seven-month gap in intelligence. With the release of newer models like Claude Fable 5.2, it's likely that gap has only widened, and the same story is likely to play out over the next few months across additional domains.
With additional safeguards against distillation and powerful compute resources becoming more difficult to find, this poses a difficult question for the Chinese labs: How can they keep up the pace and stay competitive while the odds are stacked against them?
China still holds the overall top spot in the open-weight arena with Kimi K3.1 Pro, though Western companies are bringing more performant models out as the months pass. China's second tier of open-weight models, which can often be run locally, e.g Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-27B (20 on AA), is facing competition from the American-made Thinking Machines Labs' Inkling 2 Mini (20 on AA), which was recently released. With the release of the larger (closed-weight and API only) Qwen 4 model seemingly not landing quite as well with users, it remains to be seen whether Alibaba can maintain the advantage of time, as Inkling 2 Mini was released just this week, while Qwen 3.8-27B has been out for several months.
With devices like the RTX Spark, AMD's AI Halo, and more, users are increasingly getting their own choice of running an open-weight AI, and for all intents and purposes, that usually means using a Chinese model to get the most intelligence out of your machine. However, recent developments show that smaller Western labs are also beginning to bridge that gap.
This is yet another arena in which Chinese and Western labs will want to wrest control from one another. Notably, Google has not released another series of Gemma models following Gemma 4 back in April. If a fifth generation of Google's Gemma models arrives, they'd likely be close cousins to the Gemini Neon, Carbon, Argon, and Hydrogen family, though that remains speculation until Google confirms anything official.
The silicon transition
Against the backdrop of export controls and tightening restrictions on AI distillation, Chinese AI labs are in a tough spot, and all eyes are on frontier labs like Moonshot AI, Zhipu, Deepseek, Alibaba, and Xiaomi to see if they can scale the intelligence wall that their Western counterparts currently present. More compute for training resources may be an answer, but for comparison's sake, Huawei's upcoming Ascend 950DT accelerator offers 2 PFLOPS of FP4 compute and 1 PFLOPS of FP8, while an Nvidia Rubin R200 offers 50 PFLOPS in inference and 35 PFLOPS in dense workloads. In memory capacity and bandwidth, the Ascend 950DT can offer 144GB of HiZQ 2.0 with 4 TB/s of bandwidth across a 2 TB/s interconnect. Rubin, on the other hand, offers 288GB of HBM4, with bandwidth ranging from 19.2-22 TB/s, across an NvLink interconnect at 2.6 TB/s.
If China's AI ambitions are to compete with the West, its silicon needs to either scale so the country can produce more chips to outgun a Western AI deployment with sheer numbers, or it needs to develop more advanced accelerators, while also managing the CANN software stack. The chips are figuratively, and literally, stacked heavily against China. As the race to develop Artificial Intelligence marches on, the Department of Commerce's latest measures have undoubtedly made it incredibly difficult for the country to compete.
Sayem Ahmed is the Subscription Editor at Tom's Hardware. He covers a broad range of deep dives into hardware, both new and old, including the CPUs, GPUs, and everything else that uses a semiconductor. He has worked as a professional tech journalist since 2015 and has written for Gamespot, IGN, and Dexerto.

candidato.titulo: A small galaxy's giant dark matter core challenges the standard cosmological model
candidato.resumo: New findings show that a nearby dwarf galaxy, UGCA 320, may challenge some predictions of the widely accepted cosmological model of the universe. By combining observations from the MUSE instrument with radio measurements from the MeerKAT telescope, astronomers have found that it hosts an unusually large dark matter core. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Nov. 11.

texto_fonte:
A small galaxy's giant dark matter core challenges the standard cosmological model
New findings show that a nearby dwarf galaxy, UGCA 320, may challenge some predictions of the widely accepted cosmological model of the universe. By combining observations from the MUSE instrument with radio measurements from the MeerKAT telescope, astronomers have found that it hosts an unusually large dark matter core. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Nov. 11.
Cuspy vs. core
The standard cosmological model, called Lambda Cold Dark Matter, predicts that dark matter accumulates in a sharp "cusp" at a galaxy's center. Its density rises sharply toward the center. But observations of small galaxies have shown a flat, smooth "core" instead. This mismatch is called the cusp-core problem.
To address this problem, instead of "cold" dark matter, which moves slowly and interacts through gravity, various alternative dark matter candidates have been put forward. They are warm dark matter, self-interacting dark matter and fuzzy dark matter. There's also another explanation involving ordinary matter, which says that repeated bursts of star formation and supernovae can churn up the center and push dark matter outward, flattening the cusp.
In this new study, a team of researchers led by Qinwei Yuan of Nanjing University, China, studied gas-rich UGCA 320 to measure how mass is distributed in it. They wanted to check whether it is cuspy or has a core profile.
Researchers combined radio data from the MeerKAT telescope with optical light from the MUSE and WiFeS instruments and infrared images from Spitzer. Radio data trace the galaxy's neutral hydrogen distribution; optical data trace hydrogen-alpha glow emitted by gas near star-forming regions; and infrared data show the location of the stars.
What fits the best?
Using a three-dimensional "tilted-ring" model, where the galaxy is treated as a stack of concentric rings, each with its own tilt and speed, they measured how fast the galaxy is spinning at a given distance from the galactic center to get the "rotation curve." They estimated how much of that rotation is coming from the gas and stars. After subtracting the normal matter, what remains should come from the dark matter.
Then they fit the residual rotation curve to dark matter models: the LCDM-derived Navarro–Frenk–White dark matter halo (a cuspy shape), pseudo-isothermal and Burkert models (cored shapes), and a generalized Navarro–Frenk–White model—a flexible version that measures how cuspy or cored the center really is.
They found that the observations are poorly described by the cuspy profile. Instead, models with a flatter "core" distribution provide a better fit. UGCA 320's dark matter is spread out flat in the middle. The two best-fit models gave dark matter core radii of 7.62 kiloparsecs (24,850 light-years) and 11.97 kiloparsecs (39,000 light-years).
"Such a large dark matter core radius is uncommon among dwarf galaxies," the team writes in the paper. The region that stars occupy in UGCA 320 has an effective radius of about 2 kiloparsecs (6,600 light-years). That measures the size of the region containing half of the galaxy's starlight, so it gives an idea of how big the stellar body is. Clearly, according to the models, the dark matter core extends far beyond the galaxy's stellar body.
Warm, fuzzy or self-interacting?
The team tested several explanations for UGCA 320's overly extended dark matter core. Warm dark matter (WDM) is made of lighter and faster particles and can make cores. But here, it works only if the WDM particle mass is about 0.003 keV. Other observations, however, rule out WDM particles lighter than roughly 3 to 6.6 keV, so warm dark matter fits poorly.
Fuzzy dark matter (FDM) is made of ultralight particles with wavelike behavior. It also fits the shape of the core but, again, does not fall into the required particle mass range.
Next comes self-interacting dark matter (SIDM). In this case, particles bump into each other, transmit kinetic energy from outer to inner regions and spread the center out. This fits best. The interaction strength needed for this kind of dark matter falls in the range other studies find for galaxies of this size.
They found that the normal matter scenario involving star formation episodes and supernovae also falls short. Repeated star-formation explosions and infalling clumps can flatten a cusp, but simulations show that they can only make cores of about 0.1 to 2 kiloparsecs, not in the range of 7 to 12 kiloparsecs as seen here. Existing studies have not yet shown whether supernovae could produce cores this large in a small galaxy like UGCA 320.
Therefore, self-interacting dark matter is the most promising explanation, which may pose a challenge to the standard model based on cold dark matter. "Our results are broadly consistent with the SIDM scenario, while appearing to be in tension with WDM and FDM predictions," the team concludes.

candidato.titulo: Quantum Computing 101: Can a Cat be Alive and Dead at The Same Time?
candidato.resumo: What is a qubit, why do quantum computers need to be colder than outer space, and what will they really be able to do? A plain-English guide to quantum computing, from Schrödinger’s cat to post-quantum cryptography.

texto_fonte:
The Insider Brief:
- Qubits, unlike classical bits, can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, the idea Schrödinger’s famous cat was invented to illustrate. Entanglement links qubits in ways classical computers struggle to simulate at scale.
- Superconducting qubits must be cooled to around 10 thousandths of a degree above absolute zero, far colder than outer space, to protect their fragile quantum states.
- Quantum computers won’t replace laptops, but they could transform the simulation of molecules and materials and break today’s public-key encryption, which is driving the shift to post-quantum cryptography.
Everyone in quantum gets the same questions from friends, family and colleagues outside the field. What is a qubit, really? Why do quantum computers need to be so cold? And will one replace my laptop? Here are the short answers.
A classical computer stores information in bits, each either 0 or 1. A quantum computer uses qubits. Like a bit, a qubit gives a 0 or a 1 when you measure it. Before it is measured, though, it can be in a superposition: a combination of 0 and 1 at the same time, with each outcome carrying a certain probability.
Schrödinger’s cat
In 1935, Erwin Schrödinger imagined a cat sealed in a box whose fate depends on a single quantum event. By the rules of quantum mechanics, until someone opens the box, the cat is in a superposition of alive and dead. Schrödinger meant it to show how strange quantum theory looks when stretched to everyday objects, and the paradox stuck.
Cats never behave like this, but qubits do. The catch is that superposition is fragile. Measure a qubit, or let its surroundings disturb it, and the superposition is lost: the qubit ends up behaving like an ordinary bit. The cat in the box is a reminder of how carefully a qubit has to be shielded from the outside world.
Entanglement
Qubits can also be entangled. Their states become linked, so that measuring one tells you something about the other, however far apart they are. Entanglement does not let anyone send messages faster than light, but it gives quantum computers correlations that classical computers struggle to simulate once more than a few dozen qubits are involved. Combined with superposition, it lets a quantum computer represent a number of states that doubles with every qubit added. Quantum algorithms use interference to make wrong answers cancel out and right ones reinforce, so that the right answer is the likely one when the qubits are measured.
Why so cold?
Many of today’s leading quantum computers, including the machines built at ETH Zurich’s Quantum Device Lab, use superconducting qubits: tiny electrical circuits that only behave quantum mechanically when cooled almost to absolute zero. Even a little heat jostles a qubit out of its fragile state, an effect called decoherence. So the chips sit inside dilution refrigerators, at around 10 thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. That is far colder than outer space, at about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero.
What quantum computers will and won’t do
Quantum computers are not faster versions of ordinary ones. For email, video or spreadsheets, they offer no advantage, and they will not replace laptops or phones.
Where they could change things is on specific problems that overwhelm classical machines: simulating molecules and materials for new drugs, batteries and catalysts, and possibly some optimisation problems, though the advantage there is less clear. A large enough machine could also break the public-key encryption that secures much of the internet today.which is why governments and companies are already moving to post-quantum cryptography.
Getting there means building machines with many more, and far more reliable, qubits than exist today. That is the engineering challenge labs and companies around the world are now racing to solve.
Watch the video
Dr. Anatoly Kulikov from ETH Zurich’s Quantum Device Lab walks through all of this in a 13-minute episode of The Quantum Kid, filmed live at wow² Space at ETH Zurich. It’s worth sending to anyone who has ever asked you what you actually do.
The Quantum Kid is part of Tesseract Quantum, a Swiss non-profit for quantum education, awareness and workforce development, which partners with The Quantum Insider.
Topics
Katia Moskvitch

texto_fonte:
When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job.
At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context.
Dinesh Rai
Employer:
Boston Children’s Hospital
Occupation:
Clinical AI Engineer
Education:
Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine
It was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology.
Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job.
When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein, chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s.
Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?”
For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says.
Between medicine and engineering
Rai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists.
For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients.
His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces, a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use.
That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year.
At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job.
Uncovering “clinical doppelgangers”
One project, called clinical doppelgangers, is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies.
The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance.
Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong.
Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome.
Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems.
Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them.
Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection.
“That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.”
After the prompt
In medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake?
That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says.
Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use. “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.”
An evolving career
The evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter. Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms.
What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down.
That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles.
“The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”

candidato.titulo: Salty lake water helps a zinc battery keep working at −50°C
candidato.resumo: Extreme cold can affect a water-based battery's ability to deliver electricity. Its liquid electrolyte—the fluid that carries charge—can freeze, while the charged particles moving through it slow down. Researchers have now built a rechargeable zinc battery that works at −50°C (−58°F) using saline lake water as a starting ingredient.

texto_fonte:
Salty lake water helps a zinc battery keep working at −50°C
Extreme cold can affect a water-based battery's ability to deliver electricity. Its liquid electrolyte—the fluid that carries charge—can freeze, while the charged particles moving through it slow down. Researchers have now built a rechargeable zinc battery that works at −50°C (−58°F) using saline lake water as a starting ingredient.
The brine was modified with an antifreeze additive that kept it from freezing, and a protective metal coating helped the zinc electrode withstand its salty surroundings. Together, these changes produced a pouch battery that retained 80% of its capacity after 900 charging and discharging cycles at −50°C.
The team included Huajun Tian and colleagues from the North China Electric Power University, along with researchers from Qinghai Minzu University and Beijing University of Chemical Technology. Their findings, reported in the Journal of the American Chemical Society, outline an approach that could make use of an abundant, naturally salty water supply while reducing the need for purification.
The salts help—and hurt
Water-based zinc batteries commonly use deionized water, which has almost all of its dissolved mineral ions removed to give researchers greater control over the chemistry. Salty lake water arrives with those charged particles already present.
The mixture offers a head start against freezing. Dissolved salts make it harder for water molecules to organize into ice, and their ions help carry charge through the liquid. Instead of an involved purification process, the authors describe preparing the lake water as "requiring only simple collection and filtration procedures."
But some of the dissolved ingredients, particularly chloride, encourage corrosion and unwanted reactions at the zinc surface. As the battery recharges, zinc can also accumulate unevenly, growing dendrites that can eventually cause a short circuit. How could the researchers retain the salts' useful properties while limiting the damage?
To explore the possibilities, they mixed equal volumes of lake water and propylene glycol, an antifreeze ingredient, then added a zinc salt. Tests and simulations indicated that the mixture changed how water molecules interacted with one another and with zinc ions, helping prevent freezing and reduce unwanted reactions involving water.
The electrode needed protection too, so the researchers coated it with an alloy containing indium, tin and zinc. Its microscopic, coral-like structure encouraged zinc to deposit more evenly on the surface. Under a microscope, bare zinc developed branching deposits and released hydrogen gas, while the alloy-coated electrode maintained a smoother surface with less gas production.
Putting the protection to work
At −50°C, the coating and electrolyte lasted more than 3,200 hours in a test that repeatedly moved zinc between two electrodes at a low current. This tested the stability of the zinc surfaces but did not measure the lifespan of a complete battery. For the complete device, the researchers paired the protected zinc with an electrode made from polyaniline, a conducting polymer. The pouch version reached 900 cycles at −50°C while retaining four-fifths of its capacity.
There was a trade-off, however. Some ions naturally present in the lake water competed with zinc ions for places inside the polyaniline electrode, reducing the charge it could store.
Scaling up the new battery will also require a clearer accounting of manufacturing costs, including the antifreeze and alloy coating. For now, the laboratory cells show that keeping the water's natural salts can be useful, provided the rest of the battery is designed to tolerate them.

texto_fonte:
Extensão falsa do Planilhas Google é usada para espionar e roubar e-mails do Gmail
Por Marcelo Fischer |
Uma extensão falsa do Planilhas Google (Google Sheets) está sendo utilizada por cibercriminosos para espionar e roubar e-mails do Gmail. A ferramenta maliciosa consegue monitorar até dez contas simultaneamente e pode voltar a interceptar mensagens mesmo após o usuário alterar sua senha.
O ataque foi detalhado nesta terça-feira (24) por pesquisadores da empresa de cibersegurança Gen Threat Labs. A extensão é instalada no Google Chrome sem o conhecimento da vítima pelo Remus Stealer, um malware desenvolvido para roubar informações de usuários do Windows.
Os responsáveis pelo malware afirmavam ter descoberto uma vulnerabilidade no Gmail. Em resposta ao portal Cybernews, o Google negou a existência de uma falha de segurança relacionada ao ataque.
Como funciona o roubo de e-mails do Gmail?
Após infectar o computador, o Remus modifica as configurações do Chrome para instalar a extensão e ativar o modo de desenvolvedor do navegador.
A ferramenta aparece com o nome "Google Sheets", na versão 0.5.4, e utiliza a descrição de uma extensão legítima do Google que permite editar documentos offline.
A cada minuto, a extensão maliciosa verifica se há novos e-mails não lidos nas contas do Gmail conectadas ao navegador. Os criminosos recebem informações como o endereço do remetente, o assunto e o conteúdo completo das mensagens.
Além de informações pessoais e profissionais, o ataque permite interceptar códigos de verificação e links de recuperação de senhas de outros serviços.
O roubo de mensagens é interrompido quando o usuário encerra as sessões do Gmail. Como a extensão permanece instalada no Chrome, os criminosos voltam a receber e-mails assim que a vítima acessa sua conta pelo computador infectado, mesmo com uma nova senha.
Como identificar e remover a extensão maliciosa do Chrome?
Para verificar se a extensão está instalada no navegador, siga os passos abaixo:
- Abra o Google Chrome;
- Digite "chrome://extensions" na barra de endereços;
- Procure pela extensão "Google Sheets", na versão 0.5.4;
- Caso encontre a ferramenta maliciosa, clique em "Remover".
A ativação do modo de desenvolvedor sem o conhecimento do usuário também é um sinal de alerta.
É importante destacar que apenas remover a extensão não garante a segurança do computador. É necessário realizar uma verificação com um antivírus para eliminar o malware responsável por sua instalação.
Em outro dispositivo seguro, o usuário deve alterar suas senhas, encerrar sessões ativas e verificar se existem configurações desconhecidas de encaminhamento automático de e-mails no Gmail.
